units.name: command-core
units.role: Defines what a CLI command is: its tree of subcommands, its flags, and how a typed argument list becomes one function call.
units.description: This is the heart of the library. It defines what a 'command' is: a name, a short description, some flags, maybe child commands, and a function to run. It builds the tree of commands and subcommands an end user sees, figures out which command line the user actually meant to run, checks that the required arguments and flags are present, and then calls the code the program author supplied. It also owns the plain-text help and usage screens, and a small Windows-only safety net that tells someone who double-clicked the program by accident how to use a terminal instead. It never decides what a valid combination of flags looks like, and it never decides what to suggest when someone presses Tab; it hands those questions to other parts of the library.

effects.description: Reads os.Args for the default argument list, and reads/writes os.Stdin, os.Stdout and os.Stderr as the default I/O streams for a command.
Imports the os package (for process arguments and the standard streams); the effect scanner classifies any os usage as filesystem-capable even though command.go itself never opens or writes a file.
Terminates the process with os.Exit when CheckErr sees a fatal error, and (Windows only) when the mousetrap safety check decides the program was double-clicked rather than run from a terminal.
Windows-only: sleeps for MousetrapDisplayDuration before exiting when the mousetrap help text is shown.

units.name: flag-groups
units.role: Enforces rules about which flags must, or must not, be used together.
units.description: Some programs need to say things like 'if you use --user you must also use --password' or 'pick exactly one of --json or --yaml, not both.' This unit lets a command author declare those rules by naming the flags involved, tags the flags accordingly, and then, once the user's actual flags are known, checks whether the rule was followed. If it wasn't, it produces the error message the user sees. It has no opinion about what the flags do or how the program runs; it only judges combinations.

entrypoints.name: enforceFlagGroupsForCompletion

effects.description: flag_groups.go performs no direct file I/O itself; it is declared here because the effect scanner attributes filesystem-capable I/O to this file (likely via its use of the vendored github.com/spf13/pflag FlagSet/Flag types, whose package does touch os elsewhere). Recorded for lint coverage rather than as a real behavior of this unit.

units.name: completion-engine
units.role: Decides what to suggest when a user presses Tab, and carries that answer back to whichever shell asked.
units.description: This is the part that understands shell completion as a concept: given a partially-typed command line, what are the valid next words, and should any hint be shown alongside them? It defines the vocabulary programs use to describe completions (file-only, directory-only, no-space, a fixed list, a custom function), runs whichever logic the command author registered, and answers a hidden '__complete' command that every generated shell script calls into. It also owns 'active help', small instructional hints shown during completion, and a debug log a developer can turn on to see what the engine decided and why. It does not know anything about bash, zsh, fish or PowerShell syntax; it only computes the answer and hands it back as plain data.

units.name: shell-completion-scripts
units.role: Generates the small shell scripts that let bash-v2, zsh, fish and PowerShell ask the program itself for completions.
units.description: This is how the library talks to the user's shell. For each supported shell it writes out a script, in that shell's own language, whose whole job is: when the user presses Tab, call this program's hidden completion command and show whatever it says. It walks the command tree to know the program's name and structure, but it does not decide what the suggestions are; that decision belongs to the completion engine it calls out to at Tab-press time.

units.name: doc-generators
units.role: Turns a command tree into reference documentation: man pages, Markdown, reStructuredText or YAML.
units.description: This is a separate tool built on top of the command tree: given a program's commands and their flags, it writes out reference documentation in whichever format is asked for, either as one page per command on disk or as a single stream. It reads a command's name, description, flags and subcommands to do this; it never changes the command tree, and it never talks to a shell or a terminal, only to files or a writer it's given.

violations_observed.note: ExecuteC calls c.initCompleteCmd(args), an unexported method of completion-engine's files. Legal in Go (same package) and clearly intentional, but it means command-core reaches past completion-engine's exported surface rather than through a capitalized API — recorded as a listed entrypoint rather than fixed, since nothing here is actually broken.

getCompletions calls finalCmd.enforceFlagGroupsForCompletion(), an unexported method defined in flag_groups.go. Same situation as above: a deliberate cross-file call inside one Go package, listed as a flag-groups entrypoint rather than treated as a defect.

violations_observed.location: bash_completions.go:30-33 vs bash_completionsV2.go / zsh_completions.go / fish_completions.go / powershell_completions.go
violations_observed.note: The four BashComp* flag-annotation constants live in bash_completions.go (kept in completion-engine because completions.go's dynamic engine reads them directly), while the newer per-shell generators reach the same annotations indirectly through RegisterFlagCompletionFunc/ShellCompRequestCmd instead of the constants themselves. Not a call-graph violation, but a naming wart worth a maintainer's attention: the 'bash' prefix on shared vocabulary now undersells how widely it's used.
